definitions.meaning: to take the turns off a coil or spool is to undo its windings
to wind down and loosen up after tension

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share the image of loosening something wound tight: a reel of thread, or a person after a hard day.

clue.text: He could be grounded and kept down

definitions.text: He could be grounded and kept down

parts.words: He could be grounded and kept down
parts.note: reads like a pilot or a naughty child confined, but describes a contender held beneath the favourite, a dog pinned on the ground in a fight

explanation.surface: A man who might be grounded and held back, like a punished teenager.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from dog fights: the losing dog ends up underneath, pinned to the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The contender expected to lose is the one kept down beneath the favourite, like the beaten dog in a fight.

clue.text: Weigh about two pounds and a quarter, almost

indicators.note: the word weigh is placed about, i.e. around, the pieces that follow it

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound (Latin libra), so two of them give LL
N, for north, is one quarter of the compass

explanation.surface: Instructions to weigh out roughly two and a quarter pounds of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts LL and N inside WEIGH, after its WE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearly and very close to it are synonyms of the archaic-sounding compound.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Impor-ane-? (4)': garbled OCR of what is probably 'Importance'; no scan and no wordplay recoverable

clue.text: He could be in Madrid and Paris at the same time

indicators.note: the letters of these words are taken all together at once and mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A traveller impossibly present in two capitals simultaneously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the same time' tells you to mix the letters of AND PARIS together.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Spain is someone you might well meet in its capital city.

definitions.meaning: jokingly, a pile of clothes waiting for the iron

explanation.definitionFit: A pressing demand is an urgent one, while at a laundry the creased clothes literally need ironing.

parts.note: in cricket a duck is a score of zero, i.e. nil

explanation.surface: A duck spotted floating on an English river.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck is a batsman's score of nothing in cricket, the bat-and-ball game; it has nothing to do with birds here.
explanation.definitionFit: The African waterway flowing through Egypt is a famous example of the class.

clue.text: Keen insight shown by a hundred upper-class types

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
U is the standard abbreviation for upper-class, as in 'U and non-U'
types, as in fellows or chaps, means men

explanation.surface: Sharp perception displayed by a hundred posh people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'U' for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's essays on British class speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharpness of judgment and shrewdness are what the word means.

parts.note: a light sleeper seems to be someone easily woken, but it is someone sleeping in daylight, on a couch for naps

explanation.surface: Something that holds up a person who wakes at the slightest noise.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'light-sleeper' as someone who sleeps while it is light, rather than someone easily woken.
explanation.definitionFit: A couch for resting during the daytime is the furniture that holds a person napping in daylight.

clue.text: Remove an obstruction in the river

indicators.note: the obstruction is placed in the river, inside its name

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Britain, a crossword favourite
in tennis a let is an obstruction of the serve; also an old word for hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: Clear away a blockage in a waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: LET goes in DEE, after its first letter. 'Without let or hindrance' preserves the old sense of let as obstacle.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike out or erase something is to take it away.

clue.text: Buttons said to represent danger to sailors

indicators.note: the word for Buttons is spoken out loud, giving a different spelling

parts.note: Buttons is the traditional name for a page or hotel bellboy, from the buttons on his uniform; also the pantomime page in Cinderella

explanation.surface: A man in a buttoned uniform somehow standing for a hazard at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: A bell buoy is a floating marker that rings to warn ships off a hazard, so it stands for danger to sailors; 'to represent' links the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: A floating marker with a bell tolled by the waves signals a hazard to shipping.

parts.note: seems to mean shareholders in a company, but means people who hold stock as goods in a shop

explanation.definitionFit: Shopkeepers and warehouse staff hold goods in stock, which jokingly makes them holders of stock.

definitions.meaning: an adjective meaning complete or absolute, as in an out-and-out outsider
a row of soldiers standing side by side

explanation.definitionFit: Utter as in sheer or complete, and a line as in a row of troops on parade.

clue.text: Good man gets a warning to say nothing and hide away

parts.note: a saint is a good man, abbreviated ST
sh! is the warning to be quiet

explanation.surface: A virtuous man is told to keep quiet and conceal himself.
explanation.definitionFit: To squirrel goods away in a secret place is to hoard or conceal them.

indicators.note: shuffling means the letters of feet are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: People shuffling their feet around a charity market.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair with stalls raising money, like a church fundraiser, is a bazaar.

definitions.meaning: according to the law, as a two-word phrase
a relation by marriage, such as a mother of one's spouse

explanation.definitionFit: Split as a phrase it means lawfully; joined, it names a relation gained by marriage rather than blood.

definitions.meaning: invested here means besieged: the city was besieged in the Indian Mutiny of 1857

explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested' suggests money put into capital, but its military sense is surrounded by a besieging army, as this city was during the 1857 Indian Rebellion.
explanation.definitionFit: The seat of India's government is a capital, and it was besieged by British forces in 1857.

clue.text: Erring dog ran off, played in the street

indicators.note: off means the letters of these words have gone wrong and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A stray dog ran off, while music played in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' mixes the letters of ERRING DOG RAN. The definition is loose: the answer is the one who played in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A busker cranking a barrel organ, often with a monkey, played music in the street for coins.

indicators.note: movements of the letters of the brigade's rearrange them

parts.note: the word brigade's taken with its S as a letter

explanation.surface: Troop manoeuvres being cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movements' mixes the letters of BRIGADES; here the S of the possessive counts as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten or condense a text is to cut it down.

definitions.meaning: carried out, as a plan or order
put to death, as a condemned prisoner

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'Done-to death' is a joke: read it as 'done to death', worn out, but it splits into two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Carried out describes a task performed, while put to death describes a judicial killing.

parts.note: to jack in is British slang for giving up or abandoning something
the box is informal for the TV set

explanation.surface: Giving up TV in favour of a plaything.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'jack in' a job is to quit it; 'the box' is British slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's novelty where a figure springs out of a case when the lid opens is a toy.

clue.text: He was partly known for his fasting and his leadership

definitions.text: He was partly known for his fasting and his leadership

indicators.note: only part of the words fasting and his is used, the answer hiding inside

explanation.surface: A historical figure famed for hunger strikes and political leadership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' picks the run from fastinG AND HIs; the whole clue describes the Indian leader.
explanation.definitionFit: The leader of India's independence movement famously fasted as a form of non-violent protest.

clue.text: Subject matter about right for a mundane circle

indicators.note: the subject matter is placed about, i.e. around, the letter for right

parts.note: a topic is the subject matter of a discussion

explanation.surface: A discussion topic concerning what is right.
explanation.walkthrough: TOPIC goes about R. 'Mundane' means earthly here: a line of latitude circling the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: Cancer and Capricorn name lines of latitude circling the Earth, so an earthly circle.

definitions.meaning: a harbour city in northern Israel, famous from the Crusades

explanation.definitionFit: A unit of land area, and a historic harbour town near Haifa.

clue.text: We infer a reduction in numbers

parts.note: the pieces FE and R with WE between them describe the clue words: WE placed in FER, i.e. 'We in fer'

explanation.surface: We deduce that numbers have fallen.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: split the answer as WE inside FE...R and describe it: 'We in fer', run together as 'We infer'.
explanation.definitionFit: A smaller number of things means a drop in quantity.

clue.text: Sort of brake on the turntable?

definitions.meaning: a type of brake on cars and bikes, with pads gripping a plate
a record placed on a record player

explanation.definitionFit: A flat plate gripped by pads makes one type of brake, and a vinyl record sits on a turntable.

clue.text: West End street in Paris? That's right!

indicators.note: the end of the word West, its final letter, is taken

parts.note: rue is French for street

explanation.surface: Confirming a remark about a London district and a Parisian street.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's theatre district, but here 'West End' is the end of the word West.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is correct is agreeing it is accurate.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Circus performer is irritating (4)' gives FLEA (a flea circus act that irritates), not the solution PLEA; no reading builds PLEA and no scan

explanation.definitionFit: Set off on a journey, and passed away, both fit the participle.

parts.note: P, for piano, is the musical direction meaning soft
light is illumination

explanation.surface: Gentle lighting brings about a betrothal.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'plight one's troth' is to promise marriage, so the noun can mean a betrothal.
explanation.definitionFit: An old sense of the word is a pledge or promise, as in a betrothal.

parts.note: in cricket the crease is a line marked on the pitch

explanation.surface: Next in the queue for a salary boost.
explanation.walkthrough: The crease is a white line where the batsman stands in cricket, the British bat-and-ball game.
explanation.definitionFit: A boost in wages is growth in what one is paid.

clue.text: Decided against a bid in spades, perhaps

definitions.text: Decided against a bid in spades, perhaps

parts.words: Decided against a bid in spades, perhaps
parts.note: in the card game bridge a player who declines to make a call such as one in spades says no bid

explanation.surface: A bridge player declining to call in spades.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, saying 'no bid' when your turn comes is the standard call for declining.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge, declining to call when it is your turn is the standard term for letting the auction move on.
